# Sharp vs Flat Minima and Generalisation

Flat training minima generalise better because they are stable to weight perturbations and data distribution shift. This insight drives SAM, explains SGD's implicit regularisation, and connects information theory to optimisation geometry.

## Hochreiter & Schmidhuber: MDL Argument

Flat minima require fewer bits to specify (lower description length → Occam's razor) → better generalisation. Wide basins of attraction = many equivalent weight configurations.

## PAC-Bayes Bound

E[test_loss] ≤ E[train_loss] + √(KL(Q‖P) + log(1/δ)) / (2m). Flat minima tolerate large Gaussian perturbation σ → small KL → tight bound. Sharp minima force small σ → large KL → loose bound.

## Measuring Sharpness

λ_max(H(θ*)) is the maximum curvature (sharpness). Estimated via power iteration using Hessian-vector products (no full Hessian needed). PyHessian library provides this.

## Sharpness-Aware Minimisation (SAM)

min_θ max_{‖ε‖≤ρ} L(θ+ε). Inner max solution: ε* = ρ·∇L/‖∇L‖. Then gradient at perturbed θ+ε* drives the update.

```python
# Step 1: perturb to worst-case neighbourhood
optimizer.first_step(zero_grad=True)
loss = model(x, y); loss.backward()
# Step 2: update with gradient at perturbed point
optimizer.second_step(zero_grad=True)
```

Cost: 2× gradient evaluations. Consistently improves ViT/ResNet generalisation by 1-3%.

## Why SGD Finds Flat Minima

SGD dynamics ≈ Langevin: θₜ₊₁ = θₜ − η∇L + noise. Steady-state distribution ∝ exp(−f/D), D = η·σ²/2. Wider basins have more probability mass → SGD naturally drifts toward flat minima.

## Practical Strategies for Flatness

Small batch size, higher LR exploration, SGDR restarts, SAM, SWA weight averaging, Mixup augmentation. All increase the effective diffusion temperature or explicitly penalise sharpness.
